title: The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823

sheetTitle.es: La guerra de 1812 y la doctrina Monroe, 1807–1823

summary: Find where the War of 1812 was fought, see what Spain gave up in 1819, and compare Latin America's new nations with the Monroe Doctrine of 1823.
subject: History
time: About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

map.about: This map spans North and South America. It shows national borders in 1800, with the United States shaded pink, and 52 battles from 1811 to 1815, most from the War of 1812 itself, with battlefield land that appears when you zoom in close. Three layers, off when the map opens, add the land Spain gave up in 1819, the Adams–Onís Treaty line, and ten Latin American nations labeled with the year each became independent, with symbols showing whether the United States recognized them by 1824 or later.

image.alt: North America and the Caribbean with the borders of 1800, the United States shaded pink, and the battles of the War of 1812 as blue and red diamonds of different sizes.

layers.name: Historic National Boundaries: 1800
layers.shows: Borders in 1800, before the Louisiana Purchase, with the United States shaded pink. Each pop-up names the country.
layers.source: University of Minnesota (historic national boundaries), from the MapMaker catalogue

layers.name: Land Spain gave up in 1819
layers.shows: Land Spain gave up in the Adams–Onís Treaty, including East and West Florida (green). Each pop-up gives a short note.

layers.name: Battlefield Boundaries: War of 1812
layers.shows: The land each battlefield covered (tan) and its core area (lighter tan). It draws only when zoomed in close to a battle. Each pop-up gives the battle and its size in acres.
layers.source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program

layers.name: Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819
layers.shows: The 1819 boundary with Spain as a pink dashed line in seven parts, drawn from the treaty's description and approximate. Each pop-up describes its part.
layers.source: Treaty text from the Avalon Project, Yale Law School; drawn on Natural Earth rivers

layers.name: Battles of the War of 1812
layers.shows: 52 battles from 1811 to 1815 as diamonds: blue for an American victory, red for a British victory, gray if inconclusive; bigger diamonds mean more casualties. Each pop-up gives the dates, the victor, total casualties, a short account and a casualties chart; it does not show the state or the leaders. The legend labels every opponent of the United States as British, but some battles were fought against Native nations: Tippecanoe (the Shawnee-led confederacy), Fort Mims and Horseshoe Bend (Red Stick Creeks). The pop-up's account says who fought.
layers.source: American Battlefield Trust (War of 1812 Battles map)

layers.name: Latin American independence and US recognition
layers.shows: Ten Latin American nations, labeled with the year of independence: blue circles if the United States recognized them by 1824, orange diamonds if it recognized them later (1826 to 1862). Each pop-up gives the capital, today's countries, independence and recognition.
layers.source: Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State; Library of Congress country studies

knownIssues.note: The Victor field's labels are American Side Victory and British Side Victory for every battle, so Fort Mims shows as a British victory and Horseshoe Bend as a victory over the British; both were fought against Red Stick Creek forces, and Tippecanoe against the Shawnee-led confederacy. Raised with the MapMaker team: relabel as Side A / Side B or add an opponent field.

knownIssues.where: Latin American independence and US recognition
knownIssues.note: The legend groups recognition as by 1824 or later, while question 4 asks about recognition before December 2, 1823; Brazil and Central America (1824) fall in the blue group. The pop-up date settles it. A three-way grouping (before the message, after it, later) would be clearer.

knownIssues.where: Battles of the War of 1812 pop-up
knownIssues.note: The pop-up does not show the state where a battle was fought, and the basemap has no place names, so students work out where a battle was from the coastline, the lakes and the pop-up's account. Raised with the MapMaker team: add the state to the pop-up.

knownIssues.where: Latin American independence and US recognition pop-up (US recognition date)
knownIssues.note: The pop-up shows each recognition date as a date and time in the computer's time zone, so in the United States it reads the evening before: Mexico shows 12/11/1822, 6:09 PM in Central time; the correct date is December 12, 1822. The answer notes give the correct dates.

compellingQuestion.en: How did the War of 1812 and the years after it change the United States' place in North and South America?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Cómo cambiaron la guerra de 1812 y los años siguientes el lugar de Estados Unidos en América del Norte y del Sur?

questions.task: Open The War of 1812 bookmark and use the battle diamonds to find the three main areas of fighting.
frontOfClass: Open The War of 1812 bookmark.
Open the legend: blue for an American victory, red for British, gray if inconclusive, and bigger diamonds for more casualties.
Click a diamond near the Great Lakes and read the battle's name and dates in the pop-up.
Click a diamond in each of the other clusters and use the coastline and the pop-up's account to say where it was fought.
Ask: in which three areas was most of the fighting?

steps.es: Abre el marcador The War of 1812 (La guerra de 1812).

steps.en: Click some diamonds in each group and read their pop-ups.
steps.es: Haz clic en algunos rombos de cada grupo y lee sus ventanas emergentes.

ask.en: In which three areas was most of the fighting?
ask.es: ¿En qué tres zonas se combatió más?

answer.where: The War of 1812 bookmark; Battles of the War of 1812 layer. The pop-up gives the battle's name, dates and account; it does not name the state, and the basemap has no place names. The legend gives the result by color. Students place each group from the map itself: around the Great Lakes and the border with British Canada, around Chesapeake Bay, and near the Gulf Coast and in Alabama. Some accounts mention a place, which helps.
answer.accept: Three areas named by region, read from the shape of the coast and lakes or from places the pop-up accounts mention: the Canadian border and Great Lakes; the Chesapeake Bay area around Washington and Baltimore; the South along the Gulf Coast and in Alabama. Accept the Creek War battles in Alabama as part of the southern area.
answer.text: Around Chesapeake Bay the British won at Bladensburg and burned Washington, then failed to take Baltimore. The Alabama battles were the Creek War against the Red Stick Creeks. The layer also includes Tippecanoe (November 1811), fought before the war against a Native confederacy; the pop-up may say 1 of 2 because the click also lands on the Historic National Boundaries layer (its pop-up reads Year 1800). The tan battlefield land draws only when zoomed in close, so there is none at this bookmark.

ask.en: Where and when was each battle fought, and who won? Which big battle came after the peace treaty?
ask.es: ¿Dónde y cuándo se libró cada batalla, y quién ganó? ¿Qué gran batalla fue posterior al tratado de paz?

answer.where: Battles of the War of 1812 layer, the three largest diamonds: in each pop-up, the dates under the title, the victor line (American Side Victory, British Side Victory or Inconclusive) and Total Casualties. The pop-up does not show the state; the places in the table are for the teacher. Legend: blue = American victory, red = British victory, gray = inconclusive. The table lists the five largest in case students pick a different third.

table.caption: Battles with the most casualties, from the pop-ups (the place in brackets is not in the pop-up)
rows: American victory over the Red Stick Creeks

answer.accept: The three battles with the most casualties, each with its date and result from the pop-up and a place worked out from the map or the account (the Niagara River or Canadian border for Fort Erie and Lundy's Lane); New Orleans (January 8, 1815) identified as the battle fought after the Treaty of Ghent.
answer.text: Fort Erie, New Orleans and Lundy's Lane are the three largest; news of the peace hadn't crossed the Atlantic before New Orleans. Horseshoe Bend (fourth largest) was fought against the Red Stick Creeks, not the British: the legend's British label is the layer's simplification, and the pop-up's account names Menawa and the Red Sticks.

steps.es: Abre el marcador The 1819 boundary (La frontera de 1819).

steps.en: In Map layers, turn on Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819.
steps.es: En las capas del mapa (Map layers), activa Land Spain gave up in 1819 (tierra que España cedió en 1819) y Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819 (línea del tratado Adams-Onís, 1819).

ask.en: What did the United States gain from Spain? Where does the new border follow rivers, and where does it follow straight lines? Why might a border switch from one to the other?
ask.es: ¿Qué obtuvo Estados Unidos de España? ¿Dónde sigue la nueva frontera ríos y dónde sigue líneas rectas? ¿Por qué podría una frontera pasar de unos a otras?

answer.where: The 1819 boundary bookmark. Land Spain gave up in 1819 layer: green areas East Florida (Spanish Cession) 1819, West Florida (Spanish Cession) 1819 and Spanish Cession 1819; the Notes in each pop-up say the land came through the Adams-Onís Treaty and instead of paying Spain, the United States took on $5 million, which the pop-up describes as damage caused by American citizens when they rebelled against Spain; the treaty's own terms are claims by American citizens against Spain. Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819 layer, pop-ups part 1 to part 7: the Sabine River north to 32° N; north to the Red River; the Red River west to 100° W; north along 100° W to the Arkansas River; the Arkansas upstream to its source; north to 42° N; west along 42° N to the Pacific.
answer.accept: Florida (East and West) gained from Spain, with the $5 million if read. Rivers: the Sabine, the Red and the Arkansas. Straight lines: north to the Red River, 100° W, north to 42° N, and 42° N to the Pacific. For why, accept any reasoned answer, for example that a river is a landmark both sides can find, and where no river ran the right way the treaty used lines of latitude and longitude.
answer.text: The United States already held much of West Florida. The treaty was signed in 1819 and ratified in 1821. The line is drawn from the treaty's description and is approximate, as each pop-up's note says.

title.en: New nations and the Monroe Doctrine
title.es: Nuevas naciones y la doctrina Monroe

questions.task: Open Latin America in 1825, turn on the independence layer, and compare the dates of independence and US recognition with President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823.
frontOfClass: Open the Latin America in 1825 bookmark.
In Map layers, turn on Latin American independence and US recognition.
Open the legend: blue circles recognized by 1824, orange diamonds recognized later.
Click a blue circle and read the US recognition date in the pop-up.
Write on the board: Monroe's message, December 2, 1823.
Ask: which nations had the United States recognized before that date, and why might Monroe have warned European powers to stay out?

steps.en: Open the Latin America in 1825 bookmark.
steps.es: Abre el marcador Latin America in 1825 (América Latina en 1825).

steps.en: Turn on Latin American independence and US recognition.
steps.es: Activa la capa Latin American independence and US recognition (independencia latinoamericana y reconocimiento de Estados Unidos).

steps.es: Haz clic en los círculos azules y lee la fecha de reconocimiento en cada ventana emergente.

ask.en: Which nations had the United States recognized before President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823? Why might Monroe have warned European powers to stay out of the Americas?
ask.es: ¿Qué naciones había reconocido Estados Unidos antes del mensaje del presidente Monroe del 2 de diciembre de 1823? ¿Por qué crees que Monroe advirtió a las potencias europeas que no intervinieran en América?

answer.where: Latin America in 1825 bookmark; Latin American independence and US recognition layer (legend: blue circle = recognized by the United States by 1824, orange diamond = recognized later). Six blue circles; the pop-up's US recognition line gives the date. Before December 2, 1823: Republic of Colombia (June 19, 1822), Mexico (December 12, 1822), Buenos Ayres (January 27, 1823) and Chile (January 27, 1823). Brazil (May 26, 1824) and the Federation of Central America (August 4, 1824) are blue but were recognized after the message.

table.caption: Recognized by the United States by 1824, from the pop-ups

answer.accept: The four nations recognized before the message, read from the pop-up dates (not all six blue circles); a reason for the warning that uses the map, such as new independent nations across the Americas that European powers might try to take back, or the United States wanting to be the main power in the region.
answer.text: The pop-up shows each recognition date as a date and time in the computer's time zone, so in the United States it reads the evening before (Mexico shows 12/11/1822, not December 12). The dates given here are the correct ones, and which nations fall before December 2, 1823 does not change. Monroe warned European powers not to set up new colonies in the Americas or interfere with the newly independent nations, and said the United States would stay out of Europe's wars. Haiti, independent since 1804, was not recognized until 1862 (orange diamond).

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; a sketch of the three war fronts and of the 1819 border and the area the Monroe Doctrine covered (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them); or a short talk using the map. Accept answers that use the battles to show the war ended without gains, the 1819 layers to show the United States growing and fixing its border with Spain, and the independence layer to show the new nations the Monroe Doctrine spoke for.

student.en: Answer the big question. Compare the country at the end of the war with the country in 1823, using one battle and one later layer.
student.es: Responde la pregunta central. Compara el país al final de la guerra con el país en 1823, usando una batalla y una capa posterior.

objectives: Use the battle diamonds in the Battles of the War of 1812 layer to identify the three main areas of fighting.
Click the largest diamonds to find the battles with the most casualties, their dates and results, and compare the date of New Orleans with the Treaty of Ghent.
Read the pop-ups of the Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line layers to describe what the treaty settled.
Compare the dates of independence and US recognition in the Latin American independence layer with Monroe's message of December 2, 1823.
Use the locations of the battles and the 1819 boundary as evidence to explain how the United States' position in North America changed between 1812 and 1823.
discussion: The battle diamonds cluster in three areas far apart. From the map, what was each side trying to control in each area, and why was none of them decisive?
The Battle of New Orleans was fought after the Treaty of Ghent was signed. Looking at where Ghent and New Orleans are, what does that gap tell you about how news traveled and how wars ended in 1815?

Most Latin American nations had declared independence before Monroe's 1823 message, and the United States recognized several of them. Comparing the dates on the map, was the Monroe Doctrine leading events or following them?

differentiation.support: Do question 2 from the front, reading the dates, the victor line and Total Casualties aloud, and keep the legend open on the board with the Treaty of Ghent date.
differentiation.stretch: Click the diamonds at Tippecanoe, Fort Mims and Horseshoe Bend, read in each account who fought, and explain why the legend's British label does not fit.

assessment.evidence: Strong answers use the Battles of the War of 1812 pop-ups (the victor line and Total Casualties: Fort Erie 2,628; New Orleans, January 8, 1815, after the Treaty of Ghent of December 24, 1814), the Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line pop-ups (East and West Florida; Sabine River, 100° W, 42° N) and the Latin American independence pop-ups (Mexico recognized December 12, 1822).
assessment.exemplar: The war itself changed little, but in the years after it the United States grew and began to speak for the Americas. The battles were in three areas: along the Great Lakes and the Canadian border, around Chesapeake Bay, and in the South near the Gulf Coast. One of the biggest battles, New Orleans, was fought on January 8, 1815, after the peace treaty was signed on December 24, 1814. In 1819 Spain gave up East and West Florida, and a new border followed the Sabine, Red and Arkansas rivers and then the line of 42° N to the Pacific. Before President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823, the United States had recognized four new nations, including Mexico on December 12, 1822. So the country went from fighting on its own borders to warning Europe to stay out of the Americas.

beforeYouStart.en: In the early 1800s Britain and France were at war, and both seized American ships. British warships also forced sailors off American ships into the Royal Navy, and Britain supported Native nations resisting American settlement. In June 1812 the United States declared war on Britain.
beforeYouStart.es: A comienzos del siglo XIX, Gran Bretaña y Francia estaban en guerra, y ambas se apoderaban de barcos estadounidenses. Además, los buques de guerra británicos obligaban a marineros de barcos estadounidenses a servir en la Marina Real, y Gran Bretaña apoyaba a los pueblos indígenas que se resistían a los asentamientos estadounidenses. En junio de 1812, Estados Unidos le declaró la guerra a Gran Bretaña.

readingTheMap.en: The map has no place names: click a feature to see its name. Pink shading shows the United States in 1800. Diamonds mark battles; use the legend: blue for an American victory, red for a British victory, gray if neither side won; bigger diamonds mean more casualties. The legend says British for every opponent, but some battles were fought against Native nations: the pop-up's story tells you who fought. Each battle pop-up gives the dates, the victor and the casualties. Tan shading shows battlefield land when you zoom in close to a battle. Three layers are off when the map opens: the land Spain gave up in 1819 (green), the treaty line (pink dashes, in seven parts) and the Latin American nations, shown as blue circles if the United States recognized them by 1824 and orange diamonds if later; the pop-up gives the exact date.
readingTheMap.es: El mapa no tiene nombres de lugares: haz clic en un elemento para ver su nombre. El sombreado rosado muestra Estados Unidos en 1800. Los rombos marcan las batallas; usa la leyenda: azul si ganaron los estadounidenses, rojo si ganaron los británicos y gris si ningún bando ganó; los rombos más grandes indican más bajas. La leyenda dice británicos para todos los adversarios, pero algunas batallas se libraron contra naciones indígenas: el relato de la ventana emergente dice quién combatió. La ventana emergente de cada batalla da las fechas, el vencedor y las bajas. El sombreado color canela muestra el terreno de los campos de batalla cuando te acercas mucho a una batalla. Tres capas están desactivadas al abrir el mapa: la tierra que España cedió en 1819 (verde), la línea del tratado (rayas rosadas, en siete tramos) y las naciones latinoamericanas, que aparecen como círculos azules si Estados Unidos las reconoció en 1824 o antes y como rombos naranjas si fue más tarde; la ventana emergente da la fecha exacta.

reflection.en: The war itself changed no borders. Which layer on this map shows the biggest change, and what caused it?
reflection.es: La guerra en sí no cambió ninguna frontera. ¿Qué capa de este mapa muestra el cambio más grande, y qué lo causó?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: When the map opens, the boundaries and battles are on and three layers are off: Land Spain gave up in 1819, Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819, and Latin American independence and US recognition. Students turn them on for questions 3 and 4.

misconceptions.claim: The United States won the War of 1812 and gained land.
misconceptions.response: The Treaty of Ghent returned the borders to where they were before the war, and the map shows American and British victories on every front.

misconceptions.claim: The Battle of New Orleans won the war.
misconceptions.response: It was fought on January 8, 1815, after the Treaty of Ghent was signed on December 24, 1814.

misconceptions.claim: Every battle was against British soldiers.
misconceptions.response: The battles in Alabama were part of the Creek War, fought against the Red Stick Creeks.

misconceptions.claim: Every blue circle was recognized before the Monroe Doctrine.
misconceptions.response: Blue means recognized by the end of 1824. Brazil and the Federation of Central America were recognized in 1824, after Monroe's message of December 2, 1823; the pop-up dates show it.

standards.text: Explain the causes, important events, and effects of the War of 1812
Identify the foreign policies of presidents Washington through Monroe and explain the impact of Washington's Farewell Address and the Monroe Doctrine

Examine the causes, course, and consequences of United States westward expansion and its growing diplomatic assertiveness (War of 1812, Convention of 1818, Adams-Onis Treaty, Missouri Compromise, Monroe Doctrine, Trail of Tears, Texas annexation, Manifest Destiny, Oregon Territory, Mexican American War/Mexican Cession, California Gold Rush, Compromise of 1850, Kansas Nebraska Act, Gadsden Purchase).
Analyze connections among events and developments in broader historical contexts.
Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics.
